questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: The garden in which God placed Adam was called

options.why: Gethsemane is the New Testament garden where Jesus prayed before His arrest.
options.whyWrong: Gethsemane appears in the Gospels, not in Genesis. It was the olive garden on the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed on the night He was betrayed, long after the time of Adam.

options.why: Mount Carmel is where Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal, not a garden in Genesis.
options.whyWrong: Carmel is a mountain ridge in northern Israel famous for Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18. It is never described as the garden prepared for Adam.

options.why: Genesis 2:8 states that God planted a garden in Eden and placed the man there.
Bethel is the place where Jacob dreamed of a stairway to heaven.
options.whyWrong: Bethel means 'house of God' and was named by Jacob in Genesis 28 after his dream of angels ascending and descending. It was a town and sanctuary site, not Adam's garden.

questions.hint: Think of the very opening chapters of Genesis where creation and the fall take place.
questions.explanation: In Genesis 2:8, the Lord God planted a garden in Eden in the east and placed Adam there to till and keep it. Eden was the lush home humanity lost after disobeying God's command regarding the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
questions.trap: Gethsemane is also a famous garden in the Bible, so it catches students reading too quickly. Remember Gethsemane belongs to Jesus' passion, whereas Eden belongs to creation.
questions.mnemonic: Eden = Early beginnings; Gethsemane = Garden before Good Friday.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: At the start of the Bible in Genesis, God made a special garden called Eden as the first home for Adam and Eve.
Gethsemane is a garden in the New Testament where Jesus prayed with His disciples just before His arrest. It has no connection to the creation story in Genesis.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: God placed Adam in Eden to care for creation and obey His word, showing that human life flourishes in fellowship with God.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Which two special trees stood in the midst of the Garden of Eden according to Genesis 2?
askPresets.similarAnswer: The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Joseph's brothers decided to sell him instead of killing him mainly because of the intervention of

options.why: Judah proposed selling Joseph to the Ishmaelite traders rather than shedding his blood.
Benjamin was Jacob's youngest son and had stayed at home with his father.
options.whyWrong: Benjamin was Joseph's full brother and the youngest of Jacob's twelve sons. He was not with the older brothers at Dothan when they plotted against Joseph.

options.why: Simeon was later detained by Joseph in Egypt, not the brother who suggested selling him.
options.whyWrong: Simeon never spoke up to spare Joseph's life at the pit in Dothan. Years later in Genesis 42, Joseph chose Simeon to remain bound in Egypt while the other brothers went home for Benjamin.

options.why: Levi did not propose selling Joseph; he is known earlier for avenging Dinah with Simeon.
options.whyWrong: Levi joined Simeon in attacking Shechem in Genesis 34, not in rescuing Joseph from death. In Genesis 37, Reuben stopped the immediate killing and Judah suggested the sale.

questions.hint: Reuben first kept Joseph out of immediate death in the pit, then another brother spotted the caravan of Ishmaelites.
questions.explanation: In Genesis 37:26-27, as the brothers saw a caravan of Ishmaelites heading to Egypt, Judah asked what profit they would gain by killing Joseph and concealing his blood. He persuaded them to sell Joseph for twenty shekels of silver instead.
questions.trap: Simeon stands out in the Joseph story because Joseph later bound him in Egypt, making him easy to mix up with Judah. Keep their roles distinct: Judah suggested selling Joseph, while Simeon was held as hostage later.
questions.mnemonic: Judah Jumped at the trade (selling Joseph); Reuben Rescued him from the first blow.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: When traders passed by on their way to Egypt, Judah told his brothers it was better to sell Joseph for money than to murder their own brother.
Simeon did not speak up to sell Joseph. Simeon appears prominently later in Egypt when Joseph keeps him in prison until the brothers return with Benjamin.

askPresets.label: How do I remember this?
askPresets.answer: Remember the two steps in Genesis 37: Reuben said 'Put him in the pit' (no bloodshed), and Judah said 'Sell him to the traders.'

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Which brother initially persuaded the others not to kill Joseph and to throw him into an empty pit instead?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Reuben, the eldest brother, intending to rescue Joseph secretly.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Why did Saul ask Jesse to send David to him initially?

options.why: David's fight with Goliath occurred later, after Jesse sent him with food for his brothers.
options.whyWrong: Saul did not summon David from Bethlehem to fight Goliath. In 1 Samuel 17, David arrived at the battlefront because Jesse sent him to bring provisions to his older brothers and check on their welfare.

options.why: In 1 Samuel 16, Saul asked Jesse for David to serve at court and play the lyre when a harmful spirit troubled him.
Saul offered Michal in marriage only after David defeated Goliath and won military fame.
options.whyWrong: Marriage to Saul's daughter Michal was not the reason for David's first summons. Saul later used Michal's hand in marriage as a snare after David became a celebrated warrior in Israel.

options.why: David and Jonathan's covenant friendship formed after David entered Saul's court and fought Goliath.
options.whyWrong: Saul did not send for David to find a companion for his son Jonathan. Jonathan's deep bond with David developed after David came to court and defeated the Philistine champion.

questions.hint: Recall what Saul's servants suggested when a distressing spirit began troubling the king in 1 Samuel 16.
questions.explanation: In 1 Samuel 16:14-22, a harmful spirit from the Lord tormented Saul, so his servants recommended David, a skilled lyre player from Bethlehem. Saul sent word to Jesse to send David to him, loved him greatly, and asked Jesse to let David remain in his service as his musician and armour-bearer.
questions.trap: Because David's battle with Goliath is so famous, many students assume Saul first sent for David to fight the giant. Actually, David first entered Saul's service in 1 Samuel 16 as a court musician, before Goliath appeared in chapter 17.
questions.mnemonic: 1 Sam 16 = Strings (lyre) and Service; 1 Sam 17 = Sling and Stone (Goliath).

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Before Goliath ever appeared, King Saul felt deeply troubled and needed someone to play soothing music. His servants suggested David, so Saul asked Jesse to let David work in his palace.
Goliath comes one chapter later in 1 Samuel 17, and David went to that camp on an errand from his father Jesse to deliver food to his brothers—not because Saul called him to fight.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: David's faithful service as a shepherd and musician opened the door to Saul's palace long before his public victory over Goliath.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What musical instrument did David play to soothe King Saul when the harmful spirit came upon him?

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Who arranged the false testimony that led to Naboth’s death?

options.why: Ahab coveted Naboth's vineyard and sulked, but Jezebel plotted the false accusation.
options.whyWrong: King Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard and became sullen when Naboth refused to sell his family inheritance. However, Ahab did not devise the murder plot himself; he left it to his wife.

options.why: Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name instructing elders to hire two false witnesses against Naboth.
Elijah was the prophet sent by God to condemn Ahab and Jezebel after Naboth's murder.
options.whyWrong: Elijah defended justice rather than harming Naboth. In 1 Kings 21:17-24, God sent Elijah to confront Ahab at Naboth's vineyard and pronounce judgment on his royal house.

options.why: Jehu was the commander God later used to execute judgment on Ahab's dynasty and Jezebel.
options.whyWrong: Jehu does not appear in the plot against Naboth in 1 Kings 21. In 2 Kings 9, Jehu fulfilled Elijah's prophecy by striking down Joram and having Jezebel thrown from her window.

questions.hint: Think of the queen who told the sulking king, 'I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.'
questions.explanation: In 1 Kings 21:8-13, Queen Jezebel used Ahab's royal seal to send letters to the elders and nobles of Jezreel. She commanded them to proclaim a fast and hire two worthless men to testify falsely that Naboth had cursed God and the king, resulting in Naboth being stoned to death.
questions.trap: Students often pick Ahab because he was the king who wanted the vineyard and took possession of it. Yet the text is clear that Jezebel engineered the fake trial and suborned the false witnesses.
questions.mnemonic: Ahab Ached for the land; Jezebel Jailed and killed Naboth with lies.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: King Ahab was pouting because Naboth would not sell his vineyard, so Queen Jezebel stepped in, wrote fake orders in Ahab's name, and paid liars to have Naboth stoned.
Ahab wanted the vineyard and was guilty of taking it afterwards, which is why Elijah rebuked him, but Jezebel was the one who actually wrote the letters and arranged the false witnesses.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Abuse of power and false witness cannot escape God's justice—Elijah pronounced judgment on both Ahab and Jezebel for Naboth's blood.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Why did Naboth refuse to sell or exchange his vineyard with King Ahab in 1 Kings 21?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Because it was the inheritance of his fathers, which Israelite law forbade selling permanently.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: At which brook did ravens bring Elijah food?

options.why: Marah was a desert stopping place with bitter water during the Israelites' exodus from Egypt.
options.whyWrong: Marah appears in Exodus 15 when the Israelites complained about bitter water until Moses threw a log into it. It has nothing to do with Elijah's hiding place during the drought.

options.why: God directed Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith east of the Jordan, where ravens fed him.
The brook Kishon is where Elijah slaughtered the prophets of Baal after the Mount Carmel contest.
options.whyWrong: Elijah went down to the brook Kishon in 1 Kings 18:40 to execute the prophets of Baal after fire fell from heaven on Mount Carmel. That was near the end of the drought, not where ravens fed him at the start.

options.why: The Jordan is the major river east of which Cherith lay, not the brook itself.
options.whyWrong: God told Elijah to turn eastward and hide by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan (1 Kings 17:3). The Jordan River was the landmark, not the small brook where the ravens brought bread and meat.

questions.hint: This hiding place appears right at the start of 1 Kings 17, before Elijah went to Zarephath.
questions.explanation: In 1 Kings 17:2-6, after Elijah declared a three-year drought to King Ahab, God commanded him to hide by the brook Cherith east of the Jordan. There he drank from the brook while ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and evening until the stream dried up.
questions.trap: Kishon is the other famous brook in Elijah's ministry, so students frequently swap the two. Remember Cherith came at the beginning of the drought (provision), while Kishon came at the Carmel climax (judgment on Baal's prophets).
questions.mnemonic: Cherith = Cared for by ravens; Kishon = Killing Baal's prophets.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: When drought hit Israel, God kept Elijah safe at a small stream called the brook Cherith and sent ravens to bring him food twice a day.
The brook Kishon is near Mount Carmel, where Elijah had the prophets of Baal put to death in 1 Kings 18. It is not the hiding place in 1 Kings 17 where ravens fed him.

askPresets.label: How do I remember this?
askPresets.answer: Link the timeline: Chapter 17 starts at Cherith (ravens feed Elijah); Chapter 18 ends at Kishon (Baal's prophets defeated).

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Where did God send Elijah to stay after the brook Cherith dried up?
askPresets.similarAnswer: To Zarephath in Sidon, where a widow cared for him.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Where did the Babylonian army capture Zedekiah?

options.why: Riblah was Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters where Zedekiah was judged after being captured.
options.whyWrong: Zedekiah was not captured at Riblah; he was brought there as a captive after his arrest. At Riblah in the land of Hamath, Nebuchadnezzar executed Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and then blinded him.

options.why: Babylonian troops pursued the fleeing king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho.
Babylon was the capital to which the blinded Zedekiah was later carried in chains.
options.whyWrong: Babylon was Zedekiah's final destination in exile, not where he was caught. After being blinded at Riblah, he was bound in bronze fetters and taken to Babylon until his death.

options.why: Zedekiah slipped out of Jerusalem by night through a gate near the king's garden before being caught.
options.whyWrong: In 2 Kings 25:4, Zedekiah and his soldiers broke out at night through the gate between the two walls by the king's garden. The Babylonians pursued him eastward and caught him near Jericho, not at the city gates.

questions.hint: Trace Zedekiah's escape route eastward toward the Jordan Valley after Jerusalem's walls were breached.
questions.explanation: According to 2 Kings 25:4-6 and Jeremiah 39:5, when the Babylonians breached Jerusalem, King Zedekiah fled by night toward the Jordan Valley. His army scattered, and the Babylonian troops overtook and captured him in the plains of Jericho before taking him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.
questions.trap: Riblah is the most famous place name in Zedekiah's downfall because his sons were killed and his eyes were put out there. Make sure not to confuse the place of capture (plains of Jericho) with the place of sentencing (Riblah).
questions.mnemonic: Caught on the plains of Jericho; Judged at Riblah; Imprisoned in Babylon.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: When Babylon broke into Jerusalem, King Zedekiah tried to run away toward the Jordan River, and the Babylonian soldiers caught him in the plains near Jericho.
Riblah was King Nebuchadnezzar's military camp in Syria where Zedekiah was brought for trial after his arrest. The actual capture happened earlier on the plains of Jericho.

askPresets.label: How do I remember this?
askPresets.answer: Follow the three-city chain in 2 Kings 25: Jericho (captured) -> Riblah (blinded) -> Babylon (exiled).

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What punishment did Nebuchadnezzar inflict on King Zedekiah at Riblah before taking him to Babylon?
askPresets.similarAnswer: He slaughtered Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and then put out Zedekiah's eyes.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs

options.why: Jesus frequently challenged human traditions that conflicted with God's written word.
options.whyWrong: Jesus did not appeal to oral Pharisaic traditions during His wilderness testing. Elsewhere in the Gospels, He criticized traditions of the elders whenever they set aside the commandments of God.

options.why: The Gospels do not record Jesus quoting Greek poets during His temptation.
options.whyWrong: Greek poetry appears occasionally in Paul's speeches and letters, not in Jesus' wilderness temptations. In Matthew 4 and Luke 4, Jesus grounded every reply in the Hebrew Scriptures.

options.why: Roman civil law played no part in Jesus' spiritual battle in the wilderness.
options.whyWrong: Roman law governed Judea's political administration, not Jesus' resistance to Satan's temptations. Jesus answered each test using God's covenant commands from the Old Testament.

options.why: Each time Satan tempted Him, Jesus replied 'It is written' and quoted from Deuteronomy.

questions.hint: Notice the three-word phrase Jesus repeated before each reply in Matthew 4: 'It is...'
questions.explanation: In Matthew 4:1-11 and Luke 4:1-13, the devil tempted Jesus three times after His forty-day fast. Each time, Jesus resisted by saying 'It is written' and quoting passages from the Book of Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, and 6:13).
questions.trap: Because the Pharisees were known as strict religious teachers, some students hesitate between Pharisaic tradition and Scripture. In the wilderness, Jesus relied solely on written Scripture, not oral tradition.
questions.mnemonic: Three temptations, three 'It is written' replies—all from Deuteronomy.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Every time the devil tried to trick Jesus in the desert, Jesus answered using verses from the Old Testament Scriptures.
Pharisaic tradition referred to extra human rules passed down orally, which Jesus often corrected. During His temptation, Jesus quoted God's written word from Deuteronomy.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Knowing and obeying God's word equips believers to recognize and resist temptation, even when Scripture itself is twisted out of context.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: From which Old Testament book did Jesus take all three Scripture quotations during His temptation?

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: The reaction of the priest and Levite in the parable of the Good Samaritan demonstrates the danger of

options.why: Both held sacred temple roles yet walked past the wounded traveller without helping.
Going down from Jerusalem to Jericho was merely the setting of the parable, not its moral warning.
options.whyWrong: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho sets the dangerous scene for the robbery, but Jesus never warned people against travelling from Jerusalem. His critique aimed at the hard hearts of leaders who refused to help a dying neighbour.

options.why: Jesus praised the Samaritan specifically for helping a wounded stranger.
options.whyWrong: Helping a stranger in need is the exact virtue Jesus commended in the parable, not a danger to avoid. The priest and Levite failed because they withheld help, while the Samaritan showed neighbourly love.

options.why: Pouring oil and wine on wounds was an act of mercy carried out by the Samaritan.
options.whyWrong: The Samaritan used oil and wine to soothe and disinfect the victim's wounds (Luke 10:34), which illustrates genuine care. It was not something the priest and Levite did or something Jesus warned against.

questions.hint: Contrast the respected temple positions of the priest and Levite with what they actually did on the road.
questions.explanation: In Luke 10:30-37, a priest and a Levite—men respected for serving God in the temple—saw the beaten traveller and passed by on the other side. By contrasting them with a despised Samaritan who showed mercy, Jesus exposed the emptiness of outward religious office without active love for one's neighbour.
questions.trap: Because the parable begins with 'a man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho,' students sometimes latch onto the detail about travelling from Jerusalem. That is only the story's backdrop, not its moral lesson.
questions.mnemonic: Priest and Levite Passed by; Samaritan Stopped and Served.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Even though the priest and the Levite had important religious jobs, they ignored a bleeding man on the road. Jesus used this to show that true faith must show real kindness to people in need.
The journey from Jerusalem to Jericho is just where the robbery happened. The priest and Levite were not wrong for travelling that road; they were wrong for ignoring a dying man.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: In God's kingdom, true neighbourliness is measured by mercy in action, not by religious title or ethnic background.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What question prompted Jesus to tell the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10?
askPresets.similarAnswer: A lawyer asked Him, 'And who is my neighbour?'

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: The man whose daughter Jesus raised was

options.why: Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho who welcomed Jesus into his house.
options.whyWrong: Zacchaeus appears in Luke 19 when he climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus pass through Jericho. His story is about repentance and restitution, not raising a daughter from the dead.

options.why: Jairus was the synagogue ruler whose twelve-year-old daughter Jesus raised from death.
Bartimaeus was the blind beggar outside Jericho whose sight Jesus restored.
options.whyWrong: Bartimaeus was a blind man sitting by the roadside near Jericho who cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' (Mark 10:46-52). Jesus healed his blindness rather than raising a child of his.

options.why: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and Jewish leader who visited Jesus at night.
options.whyWrong: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night in John 3 to discuss being born again, and later helped bury Jesus' body. He never asked Jesus to raise a daughter.

questions.hint: He was a synagogue ruler who fell at Jesus' feet and begged Him to come lay hands on his dying twelve-year-old child.
questions.explanation: In Mark 5:22-42 and Luke 8:41-56, a synagogue ruler named Jairus pleaded with Jesus to heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter. Even after messengers reported she had died, Jesus encouraged Jairus not to fear, entered the house, took her hand, and raised her back to life.
questions.trap: Bartimaeus is also a memorable named recipient of a miracle in Mark's Gospel, so students sometimes mix up Gospel miracle names. Bartimaeus received his sight, whereas Jairus received his daughter back from death.
questions.mnemonic: Jairus's Joy: Jesus raised his twelve-year-old daughter ('Talitha cumi').

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: A synagogue leader named Jairus begged Jesus to save his sick daughter. When she died before they reached home, Jesus went inside and brought her back to life.
Bartimaeus was the blind beggar healed outside Jericho in Mark 10. He had his own eyes opened; he did not have a daughter raised by Jesus.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Jesus told Jairus, 'Do not fear, only believe,' showing that His power is stronger even than death.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What Aramaic words did Jesus speak when He raised Jairus's daughter in Mark 5:41?
askPresets.similarAnswer: 'Talitha cumi,' which means 'Little girl, I say to you, arise.'

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Why did Jesus decline to call on His Father for legions of angels?

options.text: The disciples had already driven away the crowd.
options.why: The disciples did not drive away the armed crowd; they fled after Jesus was arrested.
options.whyWrong: Apart from one disciple cutting off the high priest's servant's ear, the disciples did not rout the arresting party. In Matthew 26:56, all the disciples left Jesus and fled once He submitted to arrest.

options.text: He lacked the authority to ask.
options.why: Jesus explicitly stated that He could appeal to His Father at once for more than twelve legions of angels.
options.whyWrong: Jesus did not lack authority or power to summon heavenly help. In Matthew 26:53, He asked Peter, 'Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?'

options.text: The Scriptures had to be fulfilled.
options.why: Jesus chose not to summon angels because the prophetic Scriptures about His suffering had to be fulfilled.

options.text: The high priest had promised to release Him.
options.why: The high priest Caiaphas sought to condemn Jesus to death, not release Him.
options.whyWrong: Caiaphas and the chief priests plotted to arrest Jesus and put Him to death (Matthew 26:3-4, 59-66). No promise of release was ever made.

questions.hint: Recall Jesus' rebuke to the disciple who drew a sword in Gethsemane in Matthew 26:53-54.
questions.explanation: When Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane and a disciple struck the high priest's servant with a sword, Jesus told him to sheath it (Matthew 26:52-54). He explained that His Father could immediately send more than twelve legions of angels, 'But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?'
questions.trap: Students sometimes think Jesus refused to call angels because He lacked power or permission to ask. Jesus' own question proves He had full authority to ask—He declined out of willing obedience to fulfill God's redemptive plan in Scripture.
questions.mnemonic: Twelve legions available, but Scripture's plan came first.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Jesus had the power to ask God for thousands of angels to rescue Him when He was arrested, but He chose not to because His suffering and death were part of God's plan promised in the Scriptures.
Jesus directly said He could ask His Father and receive over twelve legions of angels right away. His restraint was voluntary obedience, not a lack of authority.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Jesus went to the cross willingly, not helplessly, submitting to God's written plan for human salvation.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: How many legions of angels did Jesus say His Father could send if He appealed to Him in Matthew 26:53?
askPresets.similarAnswer: More than twelve legions of angels.

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: Who was accused of speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God?

options.why: In Acts 6:11, opponents secretly instigated men to accuse Stephen of speaking blasphemy against Moses and God.
Peter and John were warned not to teach in Jesus' name, not framed with this charge.
options.whyWrong: In Acts 4, the Sanhedrin arrested Peter and John for healing a lame man and preaching Jesus' resurrection, then ordered them to stop speaking in Jesus' name. They were not the ones accused in Acts 6:11 of speaking against Moses and God.

options.why: Paul was later accused in Acts 21 of defiling the temple, whereas the Acts 6 charge targeted Stephen.
options.whyWrong: Years later in Acts 21:28, crowds accused Paul of teaching against the people, the law, and the temple. However, the specific accusation in Acts 6:11 of speaking 'blasphemous words against Moses and God' was brought against Stephen—while Saul (Paul) was still watching.

options.why: Philip was another of the seven deacons, who later preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch.
options.whyWrong: Philip served alongside Stephen as one of the seven chosen to distribute food (Acts 6:5), and later evangelized Samaria in Acts 8. It was Stephen, not Philip, who was dragged before the council on false charges of blasphemy.

questions.hint: He was full of grace and power among the seven chosen deacons and became the church's first martyr.
questions.explanation: In Acts 6:8-14, men from the Synagogue of the Freedmen could not withstand Stephen's wisdom and Spirit. So they secretly bribed witnesses to claim, 'We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God,' leading to Stephen's trial and stoning in Acts 7.
questions.trap: Paul is a tempting answer because he faced similar Jewish charges later in Acts 21. In Acts 6, however, Stephen was the one put on trial—and Saul (Paul) approved of his execution.
questions.mnemonic: Stephen = Stone-killed first martyr after false charges against Moses and God.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: When opponents could not defeat Stephen in debate, they paid false witnesses to accuse him of insulting Moses and God, which led to his arrest and death.

Paul faced his own temple riot much later in Acts 21, after he had become an apostle. In Acts 6, Stephen was the one falsely charged with blaspheming Moses and God, while Paul was still on the opposing side.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Stephen stood boldly for the truth even under false accusation and forgave his killers as he died, echoing Jesus on the cross.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Which young man watched the cloaks of the witnesses and approved of Stephen's stoning in Acts 7-8?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Saul of Tarsus (who later became the Apostle Paul).

questions.label: JAMB-style practice

questions.subject: crs
questions.stem: In Ephesians 5, what command does Paul give to husbands regarding their wives?

options.text: To rule over them with an iron fist
options.why: Paul forbids harshness and calls for tender, sacrificial love rather than domination.
options.whyWrong: Paul never instructs husbands to rule harshly over their wives. Instead, he condemns bitterness and models marital leadership on Christ's gentle care and self-sacrifice.

options.text: To love their wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her
options.why: Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives with Christ's self-giving love.
Paul calls for wholehearted sacrificial love and care, far more than money alone.
options.whyWrong: While Paul mentions nourishing and cherishing one's wife in Ephesians 5:29, he never reduces a husband's duty to financial provision alone. The central command in verse 25 is self-sacrificing love patterned on Christ.

options.why: Christ purifies the church by giving Himself for her, rather than harshly demanding perfection.
options.whyWrong: Ephesians 5:26-27 shows that Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church through His own sacrificial love, not by placing impossible demands on her. Husbands are told to imitate that nourishing love, not to be harsh perfectionists.

questions.hint: Look at the standard Paul sets for a husband's love in Ephesians 5:25—it is modelled on Christ's sacrifice.
questions.explanation: In Ephesians 5:25, Paul commands: 'Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.' He goes on to explain that husbands should nourish and cherish their wives as their own bodies, just as Christ cares for the church.
questions.trap: Because Paul mentions nourishing and cherishing in verse 29, some students reduce a husband's duty to financial support. Verse 25 makes the core command clear: sacrificial, Christlike love.
questions.mnemonic: Ephesians 5:25 = Husbands love as Christ gave Himself.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Paul tells husbands in Ephesians 5 to love their wives sacrificially and selflessly—the same way Jesus loved the church and gave His life for it.

Providing financially is part of caring for a household, but Paul's command in Ephesians 5:25 goes much deeper: husbands must love their wives with self-giving devotion, just as Christ loved the church.

askPresets.label: Key lesson to remember
askPresets.answer: Christian marriage is built on mutual respect and Christlike self-sacrifice, not selfishness or domination.
